hook.text: Orange jumpsuits became standard in US prisons because they're impossible to blend into a crowd.

buildup.text: Stripping prisoners of personal clothing is a deliberate act of identity erasure. You become a number.

discovery.text: Nazi concentration camps used striped uniforms with colored badges—triangles coded race, religion, and crime.

twist.text: Some progressive prisons now let inmates wear personal clothes. Recidivism drops when identity survives incarceration.

climax.text: Guantánamo's orange jumpsuit became an iconic global symbol. ISIS used the same color on hostages as a reversal.

punchline.text: Controlling what someone wears controls who they are.

quiz.question: Why were orange jumpsuits chosen for US prisons?

details.summary: Prison clothing strips individuality to enforce institutional control. From broad arrows to orange jumpsuits, prison garb marks the wearer as property of the state. The deliberate humiliation of forced clothing reveals how deeply dress connects to dignity and identity.
details.whyItMatters: Prison uniforms expose the power dynamics embedded in clothing. Forcing specific dress on confined people is a deliberate tool of dehumanization and social control.
takeaways: Prison clothing is designed to remove individual identity
Orange jumpsuits became standard in the US for high visibility
Dress restrictions in prisons are tools of psychological control

faq.question: Why are American prison jumpsuits orange?
faq.answer: Orange was chosen because it is highly visible and rarely worn in public, making escaped prisoners easy to spot. The color also carries a stigma that reinforces the wearer's status as an inmate. Not all US facilities use orange — some use stripes or solid colors.

faq.question: Do all countries use prison uniforms?
faq.answer: No. Some countries, particularly in Scandinavia, allow prisoners to wear their own clothes as part of a rehabilitation-focused approach. The theory is that maintaining personal clothing choices helps preserve dignity and supports reintegration into society.
